To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) group-level disparities in qualification rates can persist even when groups are initially identical in every way except initial qualification densities and even when classifiers are deployed uniformly across all groups; and 2) a new intervention, which we call ``group feedback control,'' can permanently eliminate group-level qualification rate disparity.

(1) disparities in qualification rates persist in a dynamical system where agents are isolated by group membership, imitate other agents within their group, and are classified by a sequence of Bayesian-optimal classifiers, and (2) interventions can be designed to permanently eliminate such group-level disparities.

(a) persistent disparities in qualification rates between artificial subgroups can occur in a model of group-level disparities that does not posit inherent differences between groups, and (b) these disparities can be eliminated by a novel control mechanism that we introduce.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question: ``Can a machine learning classifier, trained to optimize a single metric (e.g., classification accuracy) on a single population (e.g., all applicants), be used in a fair manner across multiple subpopulations (e.g., different demographic groups) without additional interventions?'' We find that, in the absence of interventions, the answer to this question is ``No''.

The main takeaway from our work is that

group-level disparities in qualification rates can be persistent and that the dynamics of such disparities are sensitive to the structure of the underlying population and the choice of machine learning model used to classify the population.

the persistent disparities we model are a consequence of an interaction of two distinct phenomena: group-level disparities in initial qualification densities and the deployment of uniform classifiers across the entire population.
